subjects.displayTitle: Divine grace, bounty, confirmations and spiritual capacity
subjects.introduction: Rain takes the shape of whatever pool receives it. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that image for an old puzzle of the spiritual life: if grace is a free gift that never ceases, why does one heart become a garden while another stays brackish ground? Bahá’u’lláh teaches that the outpouring of the All-Bountiful has never once been interrupted, and that in this Day the Beloved Himself calls His lovers; faith and guidance are pure bestowal, while much else is received according to capacity. So the question turns back on the reader. What draws confirmation near, teaching, pure intention, love, unity, thankfulness, and what cuts it off? How does an ant become a Solomon, and why does trial increase assistance rather than withhold it? The journey leads on to the hosts of the Concourse on high, to the enkindlement that comes in teaching, to how capacity develops and differs from soul to soul, and to the forgiveness and mercy of God. Bahá’u’lláh asks God not to leave His servants to themselves [1], and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes for a student’s success by the grace and favour of God [2].

order.why: These readings describe the outpouring itself. Bahá’u’lláh writes that divine bounty has never been and will never be limited, that the outpouring of the All-Bountiful has never been interrupted, and that in this Day the Beloved Himself calls His lovers, where in past days lovers sought the Beloved. Bounty appears as rain, ocean and sunlight, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that confirmation must be as continuous as the rays of the sun. Two Tablets explain delays: a delay may be for a soul’s own good, or due to the requirements of the time. Another fears that the bounty is so great that some may stay heedless of its worth, and one adds that what is possible in these days cannot be retrieved later. Reported talks keep their distinct status. If the outpouring never ceases, what accounts for its seeming absence? How should a delay be read?
shortened: Behold how the manifold grace of God, which is being showered from the clouds of Divine glory, hath, in this day, encompassed the world. For whereas in days past every lover besought and searched after his Beloved, it is the Beloved Himself Who now is calling His lovers and is inviting them to attain His presence.

order.why: Here grace is presented as a gift that no one earns. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the blessings of the Abhá Kingdom do not depend on capacity or worthiness, for the blessings themselves become the worthiness, and that this is the Day of Grace rather than the Day of Justice. Faith, guidance and recognition are singled out as pure bestowal: one soul finds the path by the flame of a lamp while another misses it in sunlight, and souls who spent years in worship and learning remained deprived. Other passages qualify the claim. One distinguishes gifts gained through effort and capability from those that are pure bounty; another says that every bounty follows capacity except faith and certitude. Bahá’u’lláh adds that good deeds without divine acceptance are sheer nothingness. How can grace be universal and also specific? What follows from having received freely?
shortened: I bear witness that Thou hadst turned toward Thy servants ere they had turned toward Thee, and hadst remembered them ere they had remembered Thee. All grace is Thine, O Thou in Whose hand is the kingdom of Divine gifts and the source of every irrevocable decree.

The grace that is called unconditioned is also said to need a recipient. The rain of grace takes on the limits of the ground where it falls, yields nothing on brackish soil and turns pure soil into a garden; the rays of the sun appear only in a polished mirror. Iron is drawn from afar while earth remains unmoved close by. Several passages treat capacity as something to be developed: by plowing the soil, by thirst, by detachment, love and unity, and by prayer for receptiveness. Others speak of capacity that differs by nature, and of the second birth as the capacity to receive the bestowals of God. A recipient who is unaware of a gift, like a child with a gem, gains little from it. Many items here are reported talks. How do these passages fit with the claim that grace does not depend on capacity? What would developing capacity involve?

shortened: God's grace is like the rain that cometh down from heaven: the water is not bounded by the limitations of form, yet on whatever place it poureth down, it taketh on limitations---dimensions, appearance, shape---according to the characteristics of that place. In a square pool, the water, previously unconfined, becometh a square; in a six-sided pool it becometh a hexagon, in an eight-sided pool an octagon, and so forth. The rain itself hath no geometry, no limits, no form, but it taketh on one form or another, according to the restrictions of its vessel. In the same way, the Holy Essence of the Lord God is boundless, immeasurable, but His graces and splendors become finite in the creatures, because of their limitations, wherefore the prayers of given persons will receive favorable answers in certain cases.

order.why: These readings insist that human effort, however necessary, cannot succeed alone. Without confirmation every water becomes fire, learning in every science accomplishes little, education does not succeed, and no soul can draw a breath or take a step; were God’s glance withdrawn, all would return to nothingness. Healing and commerce are each given a material and a spiritual cause. Two passages see confirmation at work in history: martyrs moved by a breeze that onlookers mistook for their own power, and the sun as a single sign that conquers the world. How can a person rely wholly on confirmation and still act responsibly? What is left to the rudder?
shortened: The magnanimity of man must be heavenly or, in other words, it must be assisted by the divine confirmation, so that he may become the cause of the illumination of the world of humanity.

Many passages name what draws confirmation, often through the image of a magnet. Teaching the Cause is called the magnet of confirmation, and one reported talk says that confirmations cease when teaching is suspended. Pure intention, real love, benevolent intentions, unity and agreement, firmness, detachment, humility, patience, dignity and thankfulness are also named, together with service in schools, Assemblies, gatherings and the building of a House of Worship. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that one step taken in the path of truth brings confirmations in succession, while a foreordained bestowal still needs effort to become real. Other passages name what shuts confirmation off: discord, weariness and the search for rest, a depressed mind, pride, and conduct that blocks the outpourings for others. Any deficiency, one Tablet says, arises from our own shortcoming. Do these conditions compete with the gift of grace, or prepare for it? Which is most within reach today?
shortened: If in this day a soul shall act according to the precepts and the counsels of God, he will serve as a divine physician to mankind, and like the trump of Israfil, he will call the dead of this contingent world to life; for the confirmations of the Abha Realm are never interrupted, and such a virtuous soul hath, to befriend him, the unfailing help of the Company on high. Thus shall a sorry gnat become an eagle in the fulness of his strength, and a feeble sparrow change to a royal falcon in the heights of ancient glory.

Pure intention, real love, benevolent intentions, unity and agreement, firmness, detachment, humility, patience, dignity and thankfulness are also named, together with service in schools, Assemblies, gatherings and the building of a House of Worship. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that one step taken in the path of truth brings confirmations in succession, while a foreordained bestowal still needs effort to become real. Other passages name what shuts confirmation off: discord, weariness and the search for rest, a depressed mind, pride, and conduct that blocks the outpourings for others. Any deficiency, one Tablet says, arises from our own shortcoming. Do these conditions compete with the gift of grace, or prepare for it? Which is most within reach today?
shortened: Teaching compensates for everything because divine confirmations arrive.

The most frequent image in the compilation is transformation: a drop becomes an ocean, an atom a sun, a seed a tree, an ant a Solomon and a gnat an eagle. These passages answer a reader’s sense of weakness. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counsels looking not at one’s own capacity but at the favors of Bahá’u’lláh, and reported talks recall how Mary, through her love of Christ, was given every capacity, and how a soul unable to teach became eloquent when sent forth. Bahá’u’lláh bids the weak, the sick and the weary seek wealth, healing and utterance through His Names. A connected group turns to trial: confirmations increase with opposition, the fiercer the troubles the more intense the succor, and poverty, loss and abasement in the path of God become wealth, profit and glory. If comfort were available, one passage asks, where would distinction in striving appear? How does looking away from one’s weakness differ from denying it?
shortened: He whom the grace of Thy mercy aideth, though he be but a drop, shall become the boundless ocean, and the merest atom which the outpouring of Thy loving-kindness assisteth, shall shine even as the radiant star.

These readings record promises of assistance and accounts of it. Bahá’u’lláh writes that whoever arises to serve Him, He will arise to assist, and that God has prescribed for Himself the assistance of those who convey His Cause; the Báb gives a promise of assistance binding upon God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes the hosts of the Concourse on high arrayed and waiting for a soul to step into the arena of service, and explains elsewhere that angels signify the power of the confirmations of God. Bahá’u’lláh recalls words heard in a dream: We shall render Thee victorious by Thyself and by Thy Pen. Reported talks recount ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s journeys, where He attributes every opened door to confirmation, and a Tablet describes confirmations vouchsafed day after day to friends who raised a House of Worship in fellowship. Read promise and testimony together. What does a promise of hosts ask of the one who receives it? How might a person recognize confirmation in their own service?

Bahá’u’lláh recalls words heard in a dream: We shall render Thee victorious by Thyself and by Thy Pen. Reported talks recount ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s journeys, where He attributes every opened door to confirmation, and a Tablet describes confirmations vouchsafed day after day to friends who raised a House of Worship in fellowship. Read promise and testimony together. What does a promise of hosts ask of the one who receives it? How might a person recognize confirmation in their own service?

Bahá’u’lláh recalls words heard in a dream: We shall render Thee victorious by Thyself and by Thy Pen. Reported talks recount ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s journeys, where He attributes every opened door to confirmation, and a Tablet describes confirmations vouchsafed day after day to friends who raised a House of Worship in fellowship. Read promise and testimony together. What does a promise of hosts ask of the one who receives it? How might a person recognize confirmation in their own service?

questions: How can grace be both a pure gift that does not depend on capacity and something received according to capacity? Compare the passages saying that the blessings themselves become the worthiness and that this is the Day of Grace with those on brackish ground, the polished mirror and the outpouring that comes as soon as capacity is shown.

Why do the readings set faith, guidance and recognition apart from other bounties? Consider the passages that call guidance pure bestowal, the lamp and the sun, and the souls who spent years in worship yet remained deprived. What does this suggest about how a person should regard their own faith and the faith of others?

If the outpouring never ceases, how do the readings account for its seeming absence? Compare the passages on delay, on deprivation through heedlessness, discord, weariness and a depressed mind, and on conduct that blocks the outpourings for others.

What does the image of a magnet add to the language of grace? List the magnets the readings name, such as teaching, pure intention, love, unity and firmness, and ask whether each is a condition, a cause or a sign of confirmation.

How do the readings hold together reliance on confirmation and responsibility for effort? Consider the wind and the rudder, the foreordained bestowal that needs effort, the call for a person of action, and the counsel not to look at one’s own capacity.

What do the images of transformation, the drop and the ocean, the ant and Solomon, the gnat and the eagle, ask of a reader who feels weak? How do the passages linking confirmation with trial and opposition change the meaning of difficulty?
